fetched_contents.text: Three IoT Architecture Layers in Modern Systems Imagine a world where your alarm clock seamlessly communicates with your coffee machine, which then coordinates with your car to prepare a fresh cup of coffee just as you’re ready to leave for work. This interconnectedness, powered by the Internet of Things (IoT), has transformed our daily lives, reaching into homes, hospitals, offices, and beyond. But have you ever wondered how all these devices talk to each other so reliably? Well, it’s all thanks to modern IoT infrastructure and its three IoT layers. This IoT infrastructure design organizes devices, networks, and applications in a way that allows data to flow smoothly from sensors to cloud platforms to business systems.Yet, with so many devices connected, security challenges for the IoT are unavoidable. Each layer has its own vulnerabilities, from sensors collecting real-world data to networks transmitting it and applications using it. In this article, we’ll examine the layers of IoT architecture and discuss security from each layer’s perspective. What is IoT & IoT layers, and how IoT architecture works Let’s begin by understanding what IoT is. The Internet of Things is a system where physical devices collect data and send it to software systems over the internet. These devices can be sensors, machines, medical equipment, payment terminals, cars, or smart home devices. This entire setup is organized using Internet of Things architecture layers. In simple terms, layers of IoT architecture mean that the whole IoT system architecture is divided into clear parts (IoT architecture layers), and each part has its own job. These are also called IoT layers or Internet of Things layers. This layered approach makes complex systems easier to build, manage, scale, and secure. That is why most modern IoT architecture layers follow a structured, layered design. Let’s look at very simple business examples: * Hospital sensor: A heart-rate monitor collects patient data. The data is sent through the hospital network to a secure cloud system. Doctors see the data in a dashboard and can react instantly if something is wrong. * Payment terminal in a store: A customer pays with a card. The terminal sends the payment data through the network to the bank’s cloud system. The transaction is approved in seconds. * Travel tracking device: A GPS tracker in a delivery vehicle sends location data through mobile networks to a cloud platform. Logistics managers see the exact location in real time. Without a layered structure, these systems would be difficult to control, expensive to scale, and very hard to secure. That is why Internet of Things layers are the foundation of every reliable IoT solution today – whether in healthcare, fintech, travel, or marketplaces. Planning an IoT product? The most widely used model today is the IoT architecture 3-layers model. It is simple, clear, and works for most real-world projects. This IoT layered architecture shows how data moves from physical devices to business systems in a logical and secure way. In any modern IoT system architecture, each layer has a clear role. This is why the layered architecture in IoT is used across industries such as healthcare, fintech, travel, and marketplaces. The same logic applies to the architecture of IoT systems in both small solutions and large enterprise platforms. A well-planned IoT architecture structure helps companies reduce risks, control costs, and scale faster. Perception Layer in IoT The perception layer in IoT is the first and most physical part of the system. It is where data is created. This is also called the IoT perception layer. The main job of the perception layer in IoT architecture is to collect information from the real world. This layer is critical because if the data is wrong or insecure here, everything above it is also at risk. IoT Network Layer In modern IoT infrastructure, this layer must support millions of devices, real-time data transmission, and secure cloud connectivity. The IoT network layer is responsible for moving data from devices to cloud platforms and business systems. It acts as a bridge between physical devices and digital systems. This is where IoT and cloud computing meet. Network layer includes: * Wi-Fi; * 4G / 5G mobile networks; * gateways; * routers and communication protocols. Its main job is to: * transfer data safely; * ensure continuous connectivity; * send information from the perception layer to cloud platforms in real time. For example, a medical sensor sends patient data via Wi-Fi to a secure cloud, or a payment terminal sends transaction data over mobile networks to a bank. If this layer fails or is attacked, data can be delayed, stolen, or lost. Together, the perception layer and network layer form the foundation of the IoT data pipeline architecture, where raw device data is collected, transmitted, processed, and prepared for business use. Application Layer The application layer is where people and businesses actually use the data. This is the visible part of the IoT system architecture. It is also the core of the IoT platform architecture, where data is visualized, managed, and connected to business tools. The application layer turns raw sensor data into: * business decisions; * automated processes; * alerts and reports; * better customer experiences. fetched_contents.text: Energy-efficient architecture for perception layer of IoT system Introduction The Internet of Things (IoT) has become increasingly synonymous with modern lifestyles, particularly in domains that necessitate continuous event monitoring. The abbreviation “IoT” is now widely recognized as emblematic of contemporary technological integration, especially in applications requiring persistent observation and data acquisition. At its core, IoT encapsulates the convergence of physical objects, internet connectivity, and the automation of predefined operational tasks associated with these entities. IoT-enabled sensing systems are predominantly deployed in environments where precise and uninterrupted monitoring is imperative. Nevertheless, such settings frequently pose substantial challenges that impede direct human intervention, thereby necessitating autonomous solutions. To address these constraints, IoT devices are typically powered by battery modules and augmented with energy harvesting mechanisms, which collectively aim to prolong their functional lifespan. The determination of battery capacity and the selection of appropriate energy harvesting strategies are inherently context-dependent, influenced by the specific operational scenario and the intended application of the IoT system. These considerations must encompass a range of critical parameters, including installation costs, maintenance intervals, requisite technical expertise, and the anticipated longevity of the device. Notably, the integration of energy-intensive electrochemical sensors, if not judiciously managed, may precipitate frequent operational interruptions, escalate maintenance expenditures, and compromise overall system reliability. Electrochemical sensors can be broadly classified into several categories, including amperometric, potentiometric, impedimetric, photoelectrochemical, and electrogenerated chemiluminescence types1,2,3,4,5. Among these, potentiometric sensors—particularly coated-wire electrodes (CWEs) and ion-selective electrodes (ISEs)—are extensively utilized in the aquaculture industry for continuous monitoring applications due to their sensitivity and selectivity2,4. In typical aquaculture deployments, electrochemical sensors require additional electrical isolator circuits to facilitate the simultaneous measurement of multiple parameters within a shared water resource. Given that these probes operate in aqueous environments, they are inherently vulnerable to electrical short-circuiting, which may lead to inaccurate micro-voltage readings or, in more severe cases, catastrophic failure of the entire computing system2. Each isolator circuit generally consumes between 15 and 20 mA of current during operation, contributing to the overall power demand of the system3. fetched_contents.text: How to Optimize Energy Consumption in IoT Devices Optimizing power consumption in IoT systems is critical, especially for portable devices or devices installed in remote environments, where power is often limited and can depend on small batteries. To ensure long-lasting and efficient operation, designers and engineers must develop innovative solutions that improve energy management. Adopting optimized computing architectures and integrating advanced hardware and software strategies are essential to reduce power consumption without compromising performance. Techniques such as intelligent power management and the use of low-power communication protocols help to maximize energy efficiency. In addition, careful selection of components and the implementation of efficient processing algorithms make it possible to extend the operating life of the devices. Energy optimization is particularly relevant in industrial, home automation, and smart city applications, in which reliability and sustainability are priorities. Understanding and applying design best practices enable the development of advanced IoT solutions with low power consumption and high performance, which can improve the overall efficiency of connected systems. Choosing a power-efficient processor architecture Choosing a processor architecture is the first step in designing an energy-efficient IoT system. Two of the most popular platforms in the embedded industry are Arm Cortex-M and RISC-V. Let’s analyze their characteristics. Arm Cortex-M is widely used for its energy efficiency, thanks to an architecture optimized to perform low-power operations, and it maintains high processing capacity. An example is the STM32 Cortex-M-based microcontrollers (MCUs), which consume a few microamps in sleep mode and offer flexible power management. Nordic Semiconductor nRF52 is a series of MCUs based on Arm Cortex-M. With support for Bluetooth Low Energy, the chips are designed for ultra-low-power applications such as wearables, beacons for location, and wireless sensors. Thanks to their efficient energy management system, they can operate for years. On the other hand, the RISC-V architecture, while relatively newer, is gaining popularity due to its flexibility and ability to customize. SiFive MCUs based on the open-source RISC-V architecture allow computing units to be adapted to the specific needs of each application, eliminating unused components and reducing overall power consumption. SiFive MCUs represent an efficient solution for IoT and edge computing applications. Their modular and scalable architecture provides high design flexibility, allowing developers to optimize power consumption without sacrificing performance. The SiFive FE310, for example, is designed to minimize power consumption in sleep and standby mode and is ideal for battery-powered devices. Energy efficiency makes SiFive perfect for embedded applications in industries such as industrial automation, wearables, environmental sensors, and medical devices, where autonomy is strategic. Comparing the two architectures, Arm and RISC-V exhibit some differences. While Arm offers a proven solution supported by a wide range of software tools, RISC-V instead favors greater control over processor design, with a readiness to optimize power in specific applications. In addition to the choice of processor architecture, adopting advanced dynamic energy management techniques is essential to reduce the consumption of IoT devices. One of the most effective techniques is dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), a power management technique in electronic devices, particularly processors. It consists of dynamically adjusting the supply voltage and clock frequency according to the workload to balance performance and energy efficiency. By reducing voltage and frequency, the levels of power consumption and heat generated are also lowered, and the autonomy of mobile devices is improved. However, attention must be paid to the risk of reduced performance. DVFS is used in CPUs, GPUs, and embedded systems to optimize the ratio of power to execution speed, dynamically adapting to the workload to improve overall system efficiency. To get an idea, in wearable devices, the processor can operate at a higher frequency when processing complex data and reduce the clock in standby mode to extend battery life. Another important strategy adopted is power gating, which allows entire sections of the chip to be deactivated when they are not needed, resulting in a reduction in static power consumption. An effective method to reduce power consumption is to use low-power modes, such as deep sleep and light sleep, which can significantly extend the operating life of devices. Deep-sleep mode is one of the most energy-saving: In this state, consumption can be reduced to a few nanoamps, as the CPU is completely deactivated and only a few essential modules, such as a low-power timer or wake-up interface, remain active. Deep sleep is especially useful in IoT devices that don’t need continuous operations but need to activate only at specific times to collect and transmit data. A practical example is environmental sensors deployed in LoRaWAN networks, where the sensors spend most of their time in deep-sleep mode and wake up only when data needs to be sent. Thanks to this mechanism, energy consumption is drastically reduced, allowing the battery to last several years without the need for replacement or maintenance. A typical layered IoT architecture consists of at least three main layers: the perception layer, the network layer, and the application layer. The evidence from the IoT architecture source describes the architecture as a 3-layer model where data flows from devices through wired/wireless connections to cloud platforms and business systems [N1-F1]. Another source describes the same three-layer model as the most widely used IoT architecture model [N1-R2], and a third source also identifies the perception, network, and application layers as the core IoT architecture layers [N1-R3]. In addition, some sources mention broader four-layer models, such as sensing/perception, network/connectivity, processing-data, and user interface or application [N1-R5]. The practical implication is that the architecture is often simplified into three layers for most real-world projects, but can be expanded when additional processing or control functions are needed [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Each layer performs a distinct function in terms of data acquisition, communication, and control. The perception layer is where data is created; it collects information from the real world and is described as the most physical part of the system [N1-F1]. In building energy monitoring, this corresponds to sensors that capture electricity, water, heat, pressure, temperature, and illumination [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The network layer is responsible for moving data from devices to cloud platforms and business systems, acting as a bridge between physical devices and digital systems [N1-F1]. It supports real-time data transmission and secure connectivity, which is critical for building monitoring because high-ingest sensor data must be handled efficiently [N2-R1][N1-F1]. The application layer is where people and businesses actually use the data; it turns raw sensor data into business decisions, automated processes, alerts, reports, and better customer experiences [N1-F1].
